front: Severe aortic stenosis by 2020 ACC/AHA: peak jet velocity {{c1::≥ 4.0 m/s}}, mean gradient {{c2::≥ 40 mmHg}}, AVA {{c3::≤ 1.0 cm²}}.
State the continuity equation for aortic valve area.
back: AVA = (CSA_LVOT × VTI_LVOT) / VTI_AV = (0.785 × d²_LVOT × VTI_LVOT) / VTI_AV.

front: Where in the cardiac cycle and where anatomically is the LVOT diameter measured?
back: Mid-systole, inner-edge to inner-edge, in the parasternal long-axis view, at the annulus level.

front: Where do you place the LVOT PW sample volume for the continuity equation?
back: Approximately 2–3 mm proximal to the aortic valve. Presence of an aortic valve closing click on the trace indicates the sample volume is very close to the valve.

front: The dimensionless velocity index (VTI_LVOT / VTI_AV) is severe AS if {{c1::≤ 0.25}}. Its main advantage is being {{c2::flow-independent}}.
When must you use the full form of the Bernoulli equation for AS?
back: When LVOT velocity (v₁) > 1.5 m/s, or when AV velocity (v₂) < 3 m/s. Then ΔP = 4(v₂² − v₁²) rather than the simplified 4v².

front: How do the AS mean gradient and peak gradient relate?
back: Mean gradient ≈ 0.6 × peak gradient (or approximately 2.4 × V_max²).

front: When comparing Doppler and cath gradients in AS, which values should be compared?
back: Mean gradients only. Peak-to-peak cath gradient has no physiologic equivalent on Doppler. Peak instantaneous cath and Doppler gradients also do not occur at the same instant.

front: Why is the catheter-measured gradient typically LOWER than the Doppler mean gradient in AS?
back: Pressure recovery — downstream of the vena contracta some kinetic energy is reconverted to pressure. Doppler measures at the vena contracta (maximum gradient); cath measures a few cm downstream after recovery.

front: In which patients is pressure recovery clinically significant?
back: Moderate–severe AS with AVA ~0.9–1.2 cm² and a SMALL ascending aorta (diameter < 30 mm). Smaller aorta → more recovery → lower cath gradient / larger effective valve area.

front: Give three factors that transiently INCREASE the transaortic gradient without a true change in AS severity.
back: Anxiety, exercise, hyperdynamic state, concomitant AI, tachycardia — anything that raises stroke volume or transvalvular flow.

front: Give three factors that transiently DECREASE the transaortic gradient in true severe AS.
back: Sedation, hypovolemia, significant MR, low EF, LVH with small cavity — anything reducing forward stroke volume.

front: How is 'true-severe' distinguished from 'pseudo-severe' AS in low-flow, low-gradient AS with reduced EF?
back: Low-dose dobutamine stress echo. True-severe: peak velocity > 4 m/s (or MG > 40) with AVA < 1 cm² at peak dose. Pseudo-severe: AVA increases > 1 cm² with augmented flow.

front: What defines contractile (flow) reserve on dobutamine stress echo in AS?
back: ≥ 20 % increase in stroke volume. Absent flow reserve is a poor prognostic sign — 30-day SAVR mortality 8–30 % vs 5–8 % with reserve.

front: Define paradoxical low-flow, low-gradient severe AS.
back: EF ≥ 50 %, AVA ≤ 1 cm², but mean gradient < 40 mmHg, with low stroke-volume index < 35 mL/m². Typical patient: elderly, hypertensive, female, small LV cavity, LVH, high SVR.

front: When should you use aortic valve calcium scoring (CT) to confirm severe AS?
back: When there is discordance between AVA and gradient/velocity — especially in paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS. Severe if calcium ≥ 2000 AU (men) or ≥ 1200 AU (women).

front: How often should severe asymptomatic AS be re-imaged if not going for AVR?
back: TTE every 6–12 months.

front: What is a 'raphe' in a bicuspid aortic valve? Why is systole the key phase for identification?
back: A raphe is a fibrous ridge from congenital fusion of two commissures. A BAV with a raphe can appear trileaflet in diastole; only systole (with maximal opening) reveals only two functional cusps.

front: What is the most common bicuspid aortic valve phenotype?
back: Fusion of the right coronary and left coronary cusps (RCC–LCC) — anterior + posterior leaflets, horizontal closure line. Present in ~70 %.

front: Which BAV fusion pattern carries the highest risk of aortic dilation?
back: RCC–NCC fusion (20–30 %). Associated with greater aortopathy than the more common RCC–LCC fusion.

front: Two classic non-aortic-valve associations with a bicuspid aortic valve?
back: Coarctation of the aorta and intracranial (berry) aneurysms. Also: ~20–30 % of first-degree relatives have BAV.

front: What defines BAV aortopathy dimensions?
back: Aortic root ≥ 40 mm or ascending aorta ≥ 37 mm are considered abnormal. Growth rate typically 0.4–0.6 mm/year.

front: How does rheumatic AV disease look on echo?
back: Commissural fusion with systolic doming and leaflet thickening; TRIANGULAR AV opening in systole. Usually with concurrent mitral involvement.

front: How does senile calcific AS differ from rheumatic AS morphologically?
back: Senile: fibrocalcific masses on the aortic side of leaflets with increased stiffness but NO commissural fusion. Rheumatic: commissural fusion. Avoid direct planimetry with heavy calcification.

front: List the criteria for SEVERE aortic regurgitation.
back: Vena contracta > 0.6 cm; color jet width > 65% of LVOT; regurgitant volume > 60 mL; regurgitant fraction > 50%; EROA > 0.30 cm²; PHT < 200 ms; holodiastolic flow reversal in the proximal abdominal/descending aorta.

front: Why is a short pressure half-time (PHT < 200 ms) a marker of severe AR?
back: Rapid decline of the CW velocity slope reflects rapid equalization of aortic and LV diastolic pressures — indicating large regurgitant volume across the valve.

front: Give three echo findings distinguishing ACUTE from chronic severe AR.
back: Acute: LV NOT dilated (no time to remodel); EARLY mitral valve closure before QRS; early AV opening; fluttering of AMVL. Chronic: LV dilation, wide pulse pressure, increased E-point septal separation.

front: Name three causes of ACUTE severe AR.
back: Endocarditis, aortic dissection, blunt chest trauma.

front: What is the most common cause of MILD aortic regurgitation?
back: Hypertension.

front: Which volumetric measurement should NOT be used for cardiac output in significant AR, and what should be used instead?
back: Do NOT use LVOT stroke volume (falsely elevated by regurgitant volume). Use mitral inflow-derived stroke volume (if the mitral valve is competent).

front: Where is aortic flow reversal best interrogated on TTE for AR grading?
back: The suprasternal notch view of the descending aorta (or the subcostal window for the proximal abdominal aorta). Holodiastolic flow reversal = severe AR (analogous to Duroziez's sign).

front: List three causes of false-positive holodiastolic aortic flow reversal (mimics severe AR).
back: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA); left-arm arteriovenous fistula (e.g., dialysis fistula); stiff vasculature from long-standing hypertension.

front: Estimating LV end-diastolic pressure from an AR CW jet — how?
back: LVEDP = Aortic end-diastolic BP − end-diastolic pressure gradient (from CW AR jet, using Bernoulli: 4 × [end-diastolic velocity]²). Normal LVEDP ≈ 10–12 mmHg.

front: List three conditions commonly associated with a subaortic membrane.
back: VSD, PDA, coarctation, Shone complex, bicuspid AV, persistent left SVC, and pulmonic valve stenosis.

front: When is subaortic membrane resection indicated?
back: When at least moderate aortic regurgitation is present (jet damage progresses); in a young patient with a non-calcified AV, repair is favored over replacement.

front: What congenital syndrome typically causes supravalvular aortic stenosis?
back: Williams syndrome (elastin gene deletion, 7q11.23). Often with supravalvular PS and peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis.

front: On TEE, what is the aortic 'blind spot'?
back: The distal ascending aorta and proximal aortic arch — obscured by air in the trachea and mainstem bronchi lying between the esophagus and that aortic segment.

front: How do you distinguish a real intimal flap from an artifact in a dilated ascending aorta?
back: An intimal flap has independent oscillatory motion during the cardiac cycle. Reverberation/mirror-image artifacts move parallel to the aortic wall with no independent motion, and often have no rapid oscillatory motion.

front: What is 'Duroziez's sign' and what echo finding is it equivalent to?
back: Duroziez's = to-and-fro murmur over the femoral artery in severe AR. Echo analogue: holodiastolic reversal of flow in the proximal descending / abdominal aorta.

front: Where should the CW cursor be placed to obtain the highest AS velocity, and what maneuver may help?
back: Multiple windows: apical five-chamber, right parasternal (Pedoff nonimaging probe), and suprasternal. Use the highest velocity. Match systolic duration to the apical trace to avoid confusing MR/TR jets with AS.

front: What is valvulo-arterial impedance (Zva) and what does an elevated value indicate?
back: Zva = (mean gradient + systolic BP) / stroke volume index. It combines valvular and vascular load; a low value (< 3.5 mmHg·m²·mL⁻¹) is normal, high values suggest increased global LV afterload and worse prognosis in AS.
